questions.scenario: A wealth management firm is building a portfolio advisory system with three specialized agents: a market research agent, a risk assessment agent, and a portfolio optimization agent. When a client asks for investment advice, the system needs to coordinate all three agents — market research informs risk assessment, which constrains portfolio optimization. The firm wants a managed orchestration solution.
questions.question: Which multi-agent pattern BEST supports this sequential dependency chain?

options.text: Deploy all three as independent Bedrock Agents and let the client application call them in sequence
Use Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration with a supervisor agent that orchestrates the three specialist agents in the required dependency order
Merge all three agents into a single agent with three action groups to avoid orchestration complexity
Use Amazon SQS queues between agents to pass results asynchronously from one stage to the next

questions.explanation: Bedrock multi-agent collaboration allows a supervisor agent to orchestrate specialist agents, managing the dependency chain (market research -> risk assessment -> portfolio optimization). The supervisor handles sequencing, data passing, and error handling, providing managed orchestration of the sequential workflow.

incorrectExplanations.a: Client-side orchestration pushes complexity to the application, requires custom error handling, and doesn't leverage the managed multi-agent capabilities.
incorrectExplanations.c: Merging into one agent sacrifices specialization and makes the agent overly complex, reducing reliability and making it harder to update individual capabilities.
incorrectExplanations.d: Asynchronous SQS queues add latency and complexity for what should be a synchronous advisory workflow where the client expects a real-time response.

eliminationHints: Async queues = wrong for synchronous advisory
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Sequential multi-agent coordination = supervisor pattern

questions.examTip: When agents have sequential dependencies, use a supervisor agent to orchestrate the flow. It handles sequencing, data passing, and error recovery.

questions.scenario: An autonomous vehicle company needs a multi-agent system for their simulation platform. A perception agent processes sensor data, a planning agent generates routes, and a safety agent validates decisions. The safety agent must have veto power over any plan, and the perception and planning agents should work in parallel when possible. When the safety agent vetoes a plan, the planning agent must regenerate with updated constraints.
questions.question: Which multi-agent orchestration pattern supports parallel execution, veto authority, and iterative re-planning?

options.text: Use a simple round-robin supervisor that calls each agent in fixed order and returns the final result
Implement AWS Agent Squad with a custom orchestrator that runs perception and planning in parallel, routes results to the safety agent, and loops back to planning on veto with updated constraints
Deploy three independent agents that communicate through an SNS topic for event-based coordination
Use a Step Functions Express Workflow with parallel states for perception/planning and a choice state for safety checks

questions.explanation: AWS Agent Squad supports custom orchestration logic that can run agents in parallel, implement conditional branching (safety veto), and create iterative loops (re-planning). The custom orchestrator pattern provides the flexibility needed for complex workflows with parallel execution, authority hierarchies, and feedback loops.

incorrectExplanations.a: A round-robin supervisor executes agents sequentially in fixed order and cannot handle parallel execution, veto authority, or iterative re-planning.
incorrectExplanations.c: SNS-based event coordination is loosely coupled and cannot enforce the strict veto authority or guarantee the iterative re-planning loop completes before proceeding.
incorrectExplanations.d: Step Functions can model this workflow but lacks the agent-specific orchestration features (agent communication, shared context, tool awareness) that Agent Squad provides.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: parallel execution, veto authority, iterative re-planning
eliminationHints: SNS = too loosely coupled for strict control
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Complex multi-agent workflows with custom logic = Agent Squad with custom orchestrator

questions.examTip: Agent Squad's custom orchestrator supports parallel agent execution, conditional branching, and iterative loops — use it for complex workflows beyond simple sequential or round-robin patterns.

questions.scenario: A customer support center has two AI agents: one specialized in billing questions and another specialized in technical troubleshooting. When a customer contacts support, their query should be routed to the appropriate specialist agent. Simple queries should get a fast response, and the system should handle cases where a query involves both billing and technical aspects.
questions.question: Which agent pattern provides the SIMPLEST routing of customer queries to specialist agents?

options.text: Build a keyword-matching router that sends billing keywords to the billing agent and technical keywords to the technical agent
Use a supervisor agent that classifies the query intent and routes to the appropriate specialist agent, or to both sequentially for mixed queries
Send every query to both agents in parallel and let the user choose which response is better
Combine both agents into one general-purpose agent that handles all query types

questions.explanation: A supervisor agent uses the FM's understanding to classify intent accurately and route to the right specialist. For mixed queries, it can invoke both agents sequentially, combining their outputs. This is simpler and more accurate than keyword matching and preserves the benefits of specialization.

incorrectExplanations.a: Keyword matching is brittle and fails on queries that don't contain expected keywords. Natural language understanding (via a supervisor agent) is far more accurate.
incorrectExplanations.c: Sending every query to both agents wastes resources and puts the burden of choosing on the user, creating a poor experience.
incorrectExplanations.d: Combining into one general-purpose agent loses the benefits of specialization and makes the agent harder to maintain and update independently.

parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Query routing to specialists = supervisor agent for intent classification

questions.examTip: Supervisor agents use FM reasoning to classify and route — much more robust than keyword-based routing for natural language queries.

questions.scenario: A logistics company is designing a multi-agent system for supply chain optimization. A demand forecasting agent predicts orders, a routing agent optimizes delivery paths, and an inventory agent manages warehouse stock. The system must handle conflicting recommendations (e.g., routing agent wants to consolidate shipments but demand agent predicts urgent need) and maintain a shared view of system state.
questions.question: Which TWO design elements are MOST critical for handling conflicting agent recommendations?

options.text: A supervisor agent with conflict resolution authority that evaluates competing recommendations against business priority rules
A shared memory store (like DynamoDB) that all agents read from and write to, providing a consistent view of system state
Separate SQS queues for each agent to buffer their recommendations independently
CloudWatch alarms that trigger when agent recommendations conflict

questions.explanation: The supervisor agent (A) provides conflict resolution authority — it can weigh competing recommendations against business rules and make final decisions. The shared memory store (B) ensures all agents operate on the same system state, preventing conflicts caused by stale data. Together they address both conflict resolution and conflict prevention.

incorrectExplanations.c: Separate queues isolate agent outputs but provide no mechanism for resolving conflicts between competing recommendations.
incorrectExplanations.d: CloudWatch alarms detect conflicts after they happen but don't provide resolution mechanisms. By the time an alarm fires, decisions may have already been acted upon.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: handle conflicting recommendations and shared state
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Multi-agent conflict handling = supervisor (resolution) + shared state (prevention)

questions.examTip: Conflict in multi-agent systems needs both prevention (shared state) and resolution (supervisor authority). Neither alone is sufficient.

questions.scenario: A cybersecurity company runs a multi-agent threat detection system. A network analysis agent, a log analysis agent, and a threat intelligence agent each produce threat assessments. The company needs the system to synthesize findings from all agents into a unified threat score, but each agent has different confidence levels and may produce contradictory assessments about the same event.
questions.question: Which orchestration approach BEST handles synthesizing contradictory agent outputs into unified assessments?

options.text: Use majority voting — if two out of three agents classify an event as a threat, treat it as a threat

Implement a supervisor agent that receives all assessments with confidence scores, applies weighted reasoning based on each agent's domain relevance to the specific event type, and generates a synthesized threat score with rationale
Always defer to the threat intelligence agent since it has the most external context
Alert the human security team whenever agents disagree and wait for manual resolution

questions.explanation: A supervisor agent with weighted reasoning can evaluate each agent's assessment in context — for example, weighting network analysis higher for traffic anomalies but threat intelligence higher for known attack signatures. Confidence scores enable nuanced synthesis rather than simple voting, and the rationale provides explainability.

incorrectExplanations.a: Majority voting ignores confidence levels and domain relevance. Two low-confidence assessments shouldn't override one high-confidence assessment from the most relevant agent.
incorrectExplanations.c: Always deferring to one agent wastes the other agents' insights. Network anomalies might be invisible to threat intelligence, and log patterns might reveal threats the network agent misses.
incorrectExplanations.d: Manual resolution introduces delays that are unacceptable for real-time threat detection where minutes matter.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: synthesize contradictory outputs into unified assessment
eliminationHints: Majority voting = ignores confidence and context
Always defer to one = wastes other agents
Manual resolution = too slow for real-time
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Contradictory agent outputs = supervisor with weighted reasoning and confidence scores

questions.examTip: When agents produce contradictory outputs, a supervisor with weighted reasoning outperforms simple voting by considering confidence levels and domain relevance.

questions.scenario: A healthcare company is deploying a GenAI-powered medical coding assistant that suggests ICD-10 codes for patient encounters. Before production release, they need to validate that the system performs consistently across different medical specialties, handles edge cases correctly, and meets a 95% accuracy threshold. The validation must be automated and repeatable.
questions.question: Which deployment validation approach provides the MOST comprehensive pre-production quality assurance?

options.text: Run the system against a sample of 50 recent encounters and manually verify the suggested codes
Build an automated evaluation pipeline with specialty-stratified test datasets, edge case suites, and accuracy metrics that runs as a gate in the deployment pipeline
Deploy to production with a 5% traffic split and monitor error rates for one week before full rollout
Have three medical coders use the system for one day and provide qualitative feedback

questions.explanation: An automated evaluation pipeline with stratified test datasets ensures consistent coverage across specialties, systematic edge case testing, and quantitative accuracy measurement against the 95% threshold. Running as a deployment gate ensures no release proceeds without passing validation, making it both comprehensive and repeatable.

incorrectExplanations.a: Manual verification of 50 encounters is not repeatable, not stratified by specialty, and too small a sample to be statistically meaningful for a 95% accuracy requirement.
incorrectExplanations.c: Canary deployment catches production issues but is not a pre-production validation strategy. It risks exposing real patients to an unvalidated system.
incorrectExplanations.d: One day of qualitative feedback is neither automated nor repeatable, and doesn't provide quantitative accuracy metrics.

parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Pre-production validation = automated evaluation pipeline as deployment gate

questions.examTip: Pre-production validation should be automated, stratified by use case, and run as a deployment gate. Manual or production-based testing is insufficient for critical applications.

questions.scenario: A GenAI application uses a prompt chain where the first model extracts key facts from a document, the second model generates a summary, and the third model creates action items. Occasionally, errors in the first step propagate through the chain, producing incorrect action items.
questions.question: Which prompt chaining pattern BEST prevents error propagation?

options.text: Run all three steps in parallel to avoid sequential dependency
Add validation checks between each step that verify output quality before passing results to the next step in the chain
Use a single large prompt that combines all three steps to eliminate the chain
Retry the entire chain from the beginning whenever the final output looks incorrect

questions.explanation: Intermediate validation checks (gates) between chain steps catch errors early, preventing them from propagating downstream. If the fact extraction step produces incorrect output, the validation gate catches it before the summary step receives bad input.

incorrectExplanations.a: Running in parallel breaks the dependency chain — the summary needs facts from step 1, and action items need the summary from step 2.
incorrectExplanations.c: A single mega-prompt is harder to debug, test, and maintain. It doesn't prevent errors — it just makes them harder to isolate.
incorrectExplanations.d: Retrying the entire chain is wasteful and may reproduce the same error since the root cause isn't addressed.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: prevent error propagation in prompt chain
eliminationHints: Full retry = wasteful, may repeat error
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Error propagation in chains = intermediate validation gates

questions.examTip: Add validation gates between prompt chain steps to catch errors early. Each step's output should be verified before becoming the next step's input.

questions.scenario: A fintech company is preparing their GenAI-powered loan underwriting assistant for production launch. The system needs to handle 10,000 concurrent users, maintain sub-3-second response times, recover from model outages within 60 seconds, and comply with financial services audit requirements.
questions.question: Which TWO production readiness measures are MOST critical for this launch?

options.text: Load testing with 10,000 simulated concurrent users to verify response times and identify bottlenecks under realistic conditions
Implementing comprehensive logging of all model inputs, outputs, and decisions to an immutable audit trail for regulatory compliance
Adding a feedback button to the UI so loan officers can report incorrect decisions
Creating a runbook document that describes the system architecture for the operations team

questions.explanation: Load testing (A) validates the 10,000 concurrent user requirement and sub-3-second response time under realistic conditions — without this, the system may fail at launch. Immutable audit logging (B) is a regulatory requirement for financial services and must be in place before production. Both are non-negotiable for production readiness.

incorrectExplanations.c: A feedback button is useful for long-term improvement but is not a production readiness requirement — it doesn't address the stated launch criteria.
incorrectExplanations.d: Architecture documentation helps operations but doesn't validate performance, verify recovery, or ensure compliance — it's documentation, not a readiness measure.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: 10,000 concurrent users and financial audit requirements
eliminationHints: Feedback button = post-launch improvement, not readiness
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Production readiness = performance validation (load test) + compliance requirements (audit trail)

questions.examTip: Production readiness for regulated industries requires both performance validation (load testing) and compliance infrastructure (audit logging) before launch.

questions.scenario: An enterprise is deploying a GenAI customer service system that uses a complex prompt chain: intent classification -> context retrieval (RAG) -> response generation -> safety check. The system handles 5,000 requests per minute in production. The team needs to identify which chain step causes latency spikes, track prompt version performance across A/B tests, and detect quality degradation before customers notice.
questions.question: Which production monitoring approach provides the MOST actionable observability for this prompt chain?

options.text: Log end-to-end latency for each request and set a CloudWatch alarm when average latency exceeds the threshold

Instrument each chain step with distributed tracing (X-Ray), emit per-step latency and quality metrics to CloudWatch, and create dashboards comparing metrics across prompt versions with anomaly detection alarms
Sample 1% of requests for detailed analysis and extrapolate issues from the sample
Monitor Bedrock service-level CloudWatch metrics (invocation count, latency) and rely on the Bedrock console for troubleshooting

questions.explanation: Distributed tracing with X-Ray identifies which specific chain step causes latency spikes. Per-step metrics enable prompt version comparison in A/B tests. Anomaly detection alarms catch quality degradation proactively. This combination provides complete observability across all three requirements.

incorrectExplanations.a: End-to-end latency only tells you the system is slow, not which step is the bottleneck. It cannot support A/B prompt comparison or quality detection.
incorrectExplanations.c: 1% sampling at 5,000 rpm only captures 50 requests per minute, which may miss intermittent issues and provides insufficient data for statistical A/B test comparison.
incorrectExplanations.d: Bedrock service-level metrics don't show per-chain-step performance, prompt version comparisons, or application-level quality metrics.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: identify which step causes latency, track prompt versions, detect degradation
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Multi-step chain observability = distributed tracing + per-step metrics + anomaly detection

questions.examTip: For prompt chain monitoring, instrument each step individually with tracing and metrics. End-to-end metrics alone cannot identify which step is the bottleneck.

questions.scenario: A developer is building a Bedrock Agent that helps employees search internal databases, generate reports, and send email notifications. During testing, the agent occasionally calls the wrong tool or provides tool inputs that don't match the expected schema, causing action group failures.
questions.question: Which approach will MOST effectively reduce tool invocation errors?

options.text: Increase the agent's maximum number of reasoning turns to allow more attempts at selecting the correct tool
Write detailed, unambiguous tool descriptions that clearly specify when each tool should be used, required input parameters, and expected output format
Add a post-processing Lambda function that validates tool selections and retries with corrections when errors occur
Switch to a larger, more capable foundation model to improve the agent's reasoning ability

questions.explanation: The agent selects tools based purely on text descriptions in the system prompt. Detailed, unambiguous tool descriptions give the model clear signals about when to use each tool, what inputs are required, and what outputs to expect. This is the highest-leverage fix because it addresses the root cause — the model lacks sufficient information to make correct tool selections.

incorrectExplanations.a: More reasoning turns allow more retries but don't fix the root cause of incorrect tool selection. The agent will keep making the same mistakes with the same inadequate tool descriptions.
incorrectExplanations.c: Post-processing validation adds complexity and latency. It treats the symptom (failed invocations) rather than the cause (unclear tool descriptions). The agent should select the right tool on the first attempt.
incorrectExplanations.d: A larger model may slightly improve tool selection, but if the tool descriptions are ambiguous, even the best model will make mistakes. Better descriptions are more effective and cost less than model upgrades.

parseStrategy.keyPhrase: MOST effectively reduce tool invocation errors
eliminationHints: More turns = more retries, not fewer errors
Post-processing = treats symptoms, not root cause
Larger model = expensive, doesn't fix ambiguous descriptions
Better tool descriptions = addresses root cause directly
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Agent tool selection is driven by tool descriptions. When the agent picks the wrong tool, improve the descriptions first. This is the prompt engineering equivalent for agents.

questions.examTip: Tool descriptions are the 'prompt engineering' of agentic AI. The model chooses tools based on descriptions alone — make them precise, detailed, and unambiguous.

strategicBreakdown.whatIsBeingAsked: How to fix a Bedrock Agent that frequently invokes the wrong tools or provides incorrect parameters.

servicesInPlay.role: Agent runtime — tool descriptions drive tool selection behavior

strategicBreakdown.approachStrategy: The agent selects tools based on text descriptions. Wrong tool selection = inadequate descriptions. Improve descriptions to fix the root cause. All other options treat symptoms.
commonMistakes: Thinking a more powerful model compensates for poor tool descriptions
Adding retry logic instead of fixing the root cause
Not realizing that tool descriptions are the primary input for tool selection decisions
strategicBreakdown.timeManagementTip: Wrong tool selection → look for 'tool descriptions' in the answer options. 15 seconds.

questions.scenario: A company's GenAI-powered customer service application experiences intermittent Amazon Bedrock API throttling during peak hours. When throttling occurs, the application retries immediately, causing a cascade of failures that brings down the entire system for several minutes. The team needs to implement a resilience pattern that prevents cascading failures while maintaining service availability.
questions.question: Which resilience pattern will BEST prevent cascading failures during throttling events?

options.text: Implement a circuit breaker pattern that stops sending requests to Bedrock when the error rate exceeds a threshold, returning cached or fallback responses until the circuit resets
Add a message queue (Amazon SQS) between the application and Bedrock to buffer all requests and process them at a controlled rate
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the Bedrock model to eliminate throttling entirely
Implement retry logic with a fixed 1-second delay between attempts to prevent overwhelming the Bedrock API

questions.explanation: The circuit breaker pattern is specifically designed to prevent cascading failures. When the error rate exceeds a threshold, the circuit 'opens' and stops sending requests, returning cached or fallback responses instead. This gives the downstream service time to recover without being overwhelmed by retries. After a cooldown period, the circuit 'half-opens' to test if the service has recovered. This pattern directly addresses the described cascade.

incorrectExplanations.b: An SQS queue buffers requests but introduces significant latency for a real-time customer service application. Users expect immediate responses, not queued processing. This pattern is better suited for asynchronous workloads.
incorrectExplanations.c: Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity but involves a commitment and cost regardless of usage. It doesn't address the cascading failure pattern itself — if provisioned capacity is also exhausted, the same cascade would occur.
incorrectExplanations.d: Fixed-delay retries still contribute to the cascade. During throttling, all instances retry at the same 1-second interval, creating synchronized retry storms. Exponential backoff with jitter would be better than fixed delay, but neither addresses cascading failures as effectively as a circuit breaker.

eliminationHints: SQS queue = adds latency, not suitable for real-time customer service
Provisioned Throughput = doesn't prevent cascading failures, just reduces throttling
Fixed-delay retries = creates synchronized retry storms = worsens cascading failures
Circuit breaker = designed specifically for preventing cascading failures
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Cascading failures from retries → circuit breaker pattern. This is the textbook solution. Circuit breakers stop the cascade by halting requests when errors exceed a threshold.

questions.examTip: Circuit breaker pattern = prevents cascading failures. Retry with exponential backoff = handles transient errors. Queue = handles burst traffic. Know which resilience pattern matches which problem.

strategicBreakdown.whatIsBeingAsked: Which pattern stops immediate retries from cascading into system-wide failure during Bedrock throttling?

servicesInPlay.role: Stops sending requests during high error rates, returns fallback responses
Distractor — message queue adds latency for real-time use case

strategicBreakdown.approachStrategy: The scenario describes retry storms causing cascading failures. This is the exact problem the circuit breaker pattern solves. Eliminate options that don't prevent the cascade (SQS adds latency, Provisioned Throughput doesn't fix the pattern, fixed retries worsen it).
commonMistakes: Thinking any retry strategy prevents cascading failures (retries can worsen cascades)
Choosing Provisioned Throughput as a universal solution to throttling (it doesn't fix the retry storm pattern)
Not recognizing that circuit breakers return fallback responses rather than just failing
strategicBreakdown.timeManagementTip: 'Cascading failures' + 'retries making it worse' = circuit breaker. Pattern recognition: 15 seconds.

questions.scenario: A company is building a chatbot using Amazon Bedrock that generates long-form responses (2000+ tokens). Users are complaining about the poor experience of waiting 8-10 seconds with no visible output before the full response appears. The development team wants to improve perceived responsiveness without changing the foundation model or reducing response quality.
questions.question: Which implementation change will MOST improve the user experience?

options.text: Switch from the InvokeModel API to the InvokeModelWithResponseStream API and render tokens as they are generated
Implement client-side polling that checks for the response every 500 milliseconds
Add a loading animation with an estimated time remaining indicator
Pre-generate responses for common queries and cache them in DynamoDB for instant retrieval

questions.explanation: The InvokeModelWithResponseStream API returns tokens incrementally as they are generated, allowing the frontend to render them in real-time. Users see the first tokens within 1-2 seconds (time-to-first-token) instead of waiting 8-10 seconds for the complete response. The total generation time is the same, but perceived latency drops dramatically because users can start reading immediately.

incorrectExplanations.b: Client-side polling against the synchronous InvokeModel API doesn't help — the API only returns the complete response, not partial results. Polling every 500ms would just get repeated 'not ready' responses until the full response is available.
incorrectExplanations.c: A loading animation improves the experience marginally but doesn't address the fundamental issue. Users still wait 8-10 seconds with no useful content. Streaming provides actual content within seconds.
incorrectExplanations.d: Pre-generating and caching responses only works for predictable queries. A chatbot handles diverse, unpredictable user inputs. This approach cannot cover the long tail of possible queries and doesn't improve the experience for uncached queries.

eliminationHints: Polling doesn't return partial responses from InvokeModel
Loading animation = cosmetic, doesn't provide content sooner
Caching = only works for predictable queries
Streaming = tokens appear in real-time, drastically reduces perceived latency
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Long generation times + poor UX = switch to streaming (InvokeModelWithResponseStream). Streaming reduces time-to-first-token without changing total time.

questions.examTip: InvokeModelWithResponseStream is the answer whenever the question mentions long wait times for model responses. Streaming improves perceived latency, not actual latency.

strategicBreakdown.whatIsBeingAsked: How to improve user experience when Bedrock responses take 8-10 seconds to generate.

servicesInPlay.role: Streams tokens incrementally for real-time rendering
Distractor — caching only works for predictable queries

strategicBreakdown.approachStrategy: The problem is perceived latency (waiting with no output), not actual latency. Streaming addresses perceived latency by showing tokens as they generate. All other options either don't solve the problem or only partially address it.
commonMistakes: Thinking streaming reduces total generation time (it doesn't — same total time, but first token appears much sooner)
Choosing caching as a universal solution (only works for predictable/common queries)
Not knowing the difference between InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream

questions.scenario: A company is building an automated investment research system using Amazon Bedrock Agents. The system must: (1) gather financial data from multiple APIs, (2) analyze market trends using statistical models, (3) generate natural language research reports, and (4) route reports to appropriate analysts based on sector. Each capability requires specialized tools and prompts. The team wants to ensure each component can be developed, tested, and scaled independently.
questions.question: Which combination of design decisions supports independent development and scaling of each capability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Build a single Bedrock Agent with all four capabilities as separate action groups, using a detailed system prompt to route between them
Implement a multi-agent architecture with a supervisor agent that delegates to specialized sub-agents for data gathering, analysis, report generation, and routing
Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate four independent Lambda functions, each handling one capability without using Bedrock Agents
Deploy each specialized agent as an independent Bedrock Agent with its own model configuration, tools, and system prompt, coordinated through Amazon Bedrock multi-agent collaboration
Build all four capabilities into a single monolithic Lambda function that calls Bedrock sequentially for each step

questions.explanation: Both options implement multi-agent architectures where each capability is an independent agent. Option B uses a supervisor pattern where a central agent delegates to specialized sub-agents, enabling independent development and testing of each sub-agent. Option D uses Bedrock's multi-agent collaboration feature where each agent is independently deployed with its own configuration. Both approaches allow teams to develop, test, and scale each capability independently.

incorrectExplanations.a: A single agent with multiple action groups couples all capabilities together. Changes to one action group risk affecting others. Testing requires the full agent, and scaling applies uniformly — you can't scale the data gathering component independently of report generation.
incorrectExplanations.c: Step Functions with Lambda eliminates the agentic reasoning capabilities needed for complex tasks like analyzing market trends and generating research reports. This approach is suitable for deterministic workflows, not tasks requiring LLM reasoning.
incorrectExplanations.e: A monolithic Lambda function is the opposite of independent development and scaling. All capabilities are tightly coupled, changes require full redeployment, and the function cannot be scaled per-capability.

eliminationHints: Single agent with action groups = tightly coupled (eliminates A)
Step Functions + Lambda = no agentic reasoning (eliminates C)
Monolithic Lambda = opposite of independent (eliminates E)
Multi-agent patterns (supervisor or collaboration) = independent components
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Independent development and scaling requires separate, loosely coupled components. Multi-agent architectures (supervisor pattern or multi-agent collaboration) achieve this by making each capability a separate agent.

questions.examTip: When a question requires independent development, testing, or scaling of AI capabilities, look for multi-agent architectures over single-agent-with-many-tools.

strategicBreakdown.whatIsBeingAsked: Which architecture patterns allow each AI capability to be developed, tested, and scaled independently?

servicesInPlay.role: Central agent delegates to specialized sub-agents
Independent agents coordinated through Bedrock's native multi-agent feature

strategicBreakdown.approachStrategy: The key requirement is independence. Eliminate any option that couples capabilities together (A, E). Then eliminate the option that removes agentic reasoning (C). Both remaining options (B, D) provide multi-agent independence.
commonMistakes: Thinking a single agent with multiple action groups provides independence (it doesn't — they share the same system prompt and model)
Choosing Step Functions when the task requires LLM reasoning
Not distinguishing between supervisor pattern and multi-agent collaboration (both are valid)
strategicBreakdown.timeManagementTip: Independent development = multi-agent. Eliminate single-agent (A), monolithic (E), and non-agentic (C) immediately. B and D remain.

questions.scenario: A company is integrating an Amazon Bedrock-powered chatbot into its existing enterprise application. The company uses Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) as its identity provider. The chatbot must enforce role-based access control so that managers can access financial reports while regular employees can only access general knowledge base content. The company wants to use temporary AWS credentials, not long-lived access keys.
questions.question: Which authentication architecture meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon Cognito user pool with OIDC federation to Microsoft Entra ID, use Cognito groups mapped to IAM roles that scope Bedrock Knowledge Base access by content type
Create IAM users for each employee with embedded access keys, and assign IAM policies based on their role in the company
Deploy an EC2 instance running a custom SAML proxy that translates Microsoft Entra tokens to AWS STS temporary credentials
Use API Gateway with Lambda authorizers that validate Microsoft Entra JWT tokens and return hardcoded IAM policies

questions.explanation: Amazon Cognito with OIDC federation provides managed identity federation with Microsoft Entra ID. Users authenticate through their existing enterprise identity, and Cognito automatically issues temporary AWS credentials (via STS) based on their group membership. Cognito groups can be mapped to IAM roles that scope Bedrock Knowledge Base access by content type, implementing RBAC without managing individual user permissions. This is fully managed with no infrastructure to maintain.

incorrectExplanations.b: IAM users with embedded access keys directly violates the temporary credentials requirement. Long-lived access keys are a security anti-pattern and create significant operational overhead for provisioning and rotating credentials for every employee.
incorrectExplanations.c: A custom SAML proxy on EC2 requires managing infrastructure (instance, patching, availability) and developing custom federation logic. This adds significant operational overhead compared to the managed Cognito service.
incorrectExplanations.d: Lambda authorizers with hardcoded IAM policies require custom code to validate tokens and maintain policy definitions. This is less maintainable than Cognito's built-in group-to-role mapping and doesn't natively provide temporary AWS credentials for Bedrock access.

eliminationHints: IAM users with access keys = violates temporary credentials requirement (eliminates B immediately)
Custom EC2 SAML proxy = infrastructure to manage (high overhead)
Lambda authorizers with hardcoded policies = custom code maintenance
Cognito with OIDC federation = fully managed, built-in group-to-role mapping
parseStrategy.decisionFramework: Enterprise identity federation + temporary credentials + RBAC + least overhead = Cognito with OIDC. This is the managed AWS solution for exactly this pattern.

questions.examTip: Cognito + OIDC/SAML federation is the standard answer for enterprise identity integration with temporary credentials. IAM users with long-lived keys are always wrong when temporary credentials are required.

strategicBreakdown.whatIsBeingAsked: How to integrate enterprise identity (Microsoft Entra) with Bedrock RBAC using temporary credentials and minimal overhead.

servicesInPlay.role: Managed identity federation with OIDC, group-to-role mapping, temporary credentials
Enterprise identity provider — federated via OIDC
Role-based access control — roles assumed via Cognito group mapping

strategicBreakdown.approachStrategy: 1. Eliminate B immediately (long-lived keys violate requirements). 2. Compare remaining options on operational overhead. 3. Cognito is managed; EC2 proxy and Lambda authorizers require custom code/infrastructure.
commonMistakes: Not immediately eliminating IAM users with access keys when temporary credentials are required
Thinking a custom proxy provides less overhead than a managed service
Not recognizing Cognito's built-in group-to-role mapping for RBAC
strategicBreakdown.timeManagementTip: Temporary credentials requirement eliminates B instantly. 'Least overhead' points to managed service (Cognito). Two-step elimination: 20 seconds.
